policy_title: Tackle Child Poverty by Removing Two-Child Limit and Benefit Cap
stated: Tackle child poverty by removing the two-child limit and the benefit cap. Repair the broken benefits safety net by: Reducing the wait for the first payment of Universal Credit from five weeks to five days. Scrapping the bedroom tax. Replacing the sanctions regime with an incentive-based scheme to help people into work. Ending the young parent penalty for under-25s by restoring the full rate of Universal Credit for all parents regardless of age.

bearing_set.reason: Removing the two-child limit, benefit cap, reducing UC wait times, and restoring under-25 UC rates directly raises disposable income for lower-income families, materially affecting their ability to afford essentials.

Scrapping the bedroom tax directly reduces the housing-benefit deduction imposed on social tenants with spare rooms, materially affecting whether those households can afford to remain in their current social home.

Replacing the punitive sanctions regime with an incentive-based scheme is explicitly designed to affect employment entry and quality; benefit-cap removal also affects in-work poverty for larger families in low-wage work.

Reducing child poverty through income transfers has a well-evidenced direct effect on the attainment gap for poorer pupils — one of O7's explicit indicators — via improved material conditions and school readiness.

Removing the two-child limit (~£1.7bn/yr saving reversed), benefit cap, bedroom tax, and restoring full UC for under-25 parents represent material unfunded spending increases that widen the funded/borrowed balance, earning a real worsens verdict here.

All measures are specifically targeted at the bottom of the income distribution, narrowing the gap between the poorest families (especially those with multiple children) and the rest, giving a clear improves verdict on the income-gap indicator.

membership_note: Policy is a multi-element welfare reform package with four genuine bearings: it improves cost-of-living conditions and in-work poverty for low-income households, narrows inequality, and imposes a material public-finance cost. No other fundamentals clear the non-negligible bar — the educational attainment effect is real but too indirect to earn O7, and there is no direct safety, liberty, or housing-supply mechanism.
